title: Aash-e anar
subtitle: Persian pomegranate and walnut soup
excerpt: Aash-e anar is a Persian pomegranate soup with walnuts, lentils, and fresh herbs, thickened with rice and finished with a tart pomegranate and date syrup glaze. It is a sweet-sour-earthy soup with a vivid ruby colour from the pomegranate, served as a starter or light main.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Aash-e anar documented as an autumn soup made when pomegranates are in season. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). The walnut-pomegranate combination described as a classic Persian pairing found across soups, stews, and dips.

recipe.batchNotes: Makes well in large quantities. Keeps in the fridge for three days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to two days ahead. The soup thickens on standing; add water to loosen when reheating.

content.text: Aash-e anar is a Persian autumn soup with pomegranate, walnuts, lentils, and herbs. The lentils and rice give it body; the parsley and spring onion add brightness; and the pomegranate seeds at the end add crunch and colour. Date syrup gives the deep, slightly sweet sharpness that pomegranate treacle provides in the original.

items.prepNote: as a substitute for pomegranate molasses

content.text: Heat {{olive-oil}} in a large pot over a medium heat. Add {{onion}} and cook for ten minutes until soft and golden.

Add {{lentils-green}}, {{long-grain-rice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, and 1.2 litres of water. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 25 minutes until the lentils and rice are tender.

Stir in most of the {{pomegranate}} seeds (reserve some for garnish), {{walnuts}}, {{spring-onion}}, {{parsley-flat}}, {{coriander}}, {{date-syrup}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Simmer for ten more minutes. Taste: the soup should be noticeably sweet-sour. Adjust with more date syrup or {{caster-sugar}} as needed.
Serve in bowls with the reserved pomegranate seeds scattered over the top.

items.cause: Pomegranate seeds were very sour or date syrup quantity too high
items.fix: Add a teaspoon of sugar and stir. Taste after each addition. The flavour should be balanced between sour, sweet, and savoury.

items.symptom: The soup has become very thick
items.cause: Rice and lentils absorb a lot of liquid as they cool
items.fix: Add water to loosen, a ladle at a time. Reheat gently and adjust seasoning.

items.symptom: The walnut flavour is too bitter
items.cause: Old walnuts can be very bitter
items.fix: Use freshly bought walnuts. Taste before adding: they should be mild. Toasting them briefly in a dry pan removes some bitterness.
Add parsley and coriander only in the last ten minutes. Reserve a small amount to scatter raw over at serving for colour.

content.text: Aash-e anar is an autumn soup tied to the pomegranate season in Iran. The pomegranate has deep meaning in Iranian culture: it appears in art, poetry, and ceremony. The walnut and pomegranate pairing is a classic Persian combination, also seen in fesenjan stew: the bitterness of walnuts and the sharp sweetness of pomegranate work together. The soup can be made without meat (as here) or with small lamb meatballs added to the pot. The sweet-sour-savoury balance is stronger than in most Western soups.
